criteria.quote: "Rain hits Charmander’s tail: steam rises, flame stays lit."
criteria.revision: Open with the contradiction as a direct question: "Rain makes steam spout from Charmander’s tail—so why can a healthy flame still burn when wet?" This preserves the evidence while making the viewer wait for the health clue.

criteria.quote: "But that tail flame also indicates its life force."
criteria.revision: Make the health detail more concrete in the same scene: change it to "Charmander’s tail flame indicates its life force: when it is weak, the flame burns weakly too." This ties the rain paradox to a Charmander-specific rule earlier.

criteria.quote: "If rain makes Charmander’s tail steam, how can its flame stay lit?"
criteria.revision: Do not answer the loop in the first scene with "flame stays lit." Instead say, "Rain hits its tail—and steam is said to spout from the tip." Hold the fact that a healthy flame can burn while wet until the reveal.

criteria.quote: "Charmander prefers hot places, so rain looks like trouble."
criteria.revision: Replace this low-stakes detour with a progression from observation to consequence: after the steam scene, go directly to "Its tail flame indicates its life force." Then reveal, "If it is weak, the flame burns weakly." This makes each beat move closer to why surviving wetness matters.

criteria.quote: "A healthy Charmander’s flame burns vigorously, even when it gets wet."
criteria.revision: Make this the final factual reveal rather than placing a summary scene after it. Follow the weak-flame line immediately with: "But being wet is not the same as being weak: if Charmander is healthy, its flame burns vigorously even when it gets a bit wet."

criteria.quote: "THIS FLAME MEANS LIFE" / "WEAK FLAME, WEAK LIFE" / "THE FLAME SHOWS ITS CONDITION"
criteria.revision: Merge the life-force and weak-flame scenes into one beat, since both establish the same health-reading idea. Use the freed scene for the documented contrast that the flame can also indicate emotion: it wavers when Charmander is happy and blazes when enraged.

criteria.quote: "The steam is only half the clue: Charmander’s tail reflects its life force, and a healthy flame burns vigorously even when wet."
criteria.revision: End on the evidence-backed reversal, not another restatement: "Steam does not tell us the flame is failing. Charmander’s health does: when it is healthy, its tail flame can burn vigorously even when it gets a bit wet."

criteria.quote: "Life gauge or mood gauge: what defines Charmander’s flame?"
criteria.revision: Replace the false either-or framing with a real evidence-based split: "What would you read first from Charmander’s flame: its health, or its mood?" Its flame is documented as indicating life force and emotions, so both positions are credible.
